chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Deleveraging Process, Dalio's Four Levers

lessons.title: What Happens When Debt Cannot Be Serviced: The Onset of Deleveraging

body.text: A deleveraging begins the moment lenders stop believing that extending more credit is safe. From that moment, unless it is deliberately managed, the process feeds on itself: forced selling pushes prices down, falling prices shrink collateral, and shrinking collateral triggers more forced selling.

children.text: Chapter 2 ended with an economy that has exhausted MP1 and MP2, and is still watching its debt service ratio climb. This lesson picks up exactly there and asks what actually happens next, mechanically, once conventional tools stop working. This is the onset of deleveraging: not a policy choice, but a self-reinforcing spiral that begins the moment lenders' confidence breaks. Lessons 2 and 3 of this chapter cover the four levers used to manage that spiral once it starts; this lesson covers why it starts, and why it is dangerous if left alone.
The Credit Event: When Lenders Stop Extending

Throughout the bubble phase covered in Chapter 2, lenders kept extending credit because rising collateral values made it look safe to do so. A credit event is the moment that assumption breaks, usually triggered by something specific and visible: a large, well-known borrower defaulting, a sharper-than-expected rate hike, or simply enough bad news accumulating that lenders start questioning valuations they had been comfortable with for years. Once that happens, refinancing that used to be automatic suddenly is not. Borrowers who were never planning to actually repay principal, only to roll it over indefinitely, discover they cannot. They are forced to sell assets to raise cash, and that selling is where the self-reinforcing part of a deleveraging actually begins.
A Real Trigger: India's 2018 IL&FS Default

In mid-2018, Infrastructure Leasing & Financial Services (IL&FS), a large, systemically connected infrastructure financing group, began defaulting on its commercial paper and bond repayments. Because IL&FS had been considered a safe, high-quality borrower, its default triggered a sharp loss of confidence across the wider NBFC and housing finance sector, not just in IL&FS itself. Mutual funds pulled back from NBFC commercial paper, NBFCs found it harder and costlier to roll over their own short-term borrowing, and credit to sectors that depended heavily on NBFC financing, real estate and auto among them, tightened sharply through 2019. This lesson uses IL&FS only as a compact illustration of a credit event triggering contagion; Chapter 5 covers its role in India's broader credit cycle in full.
Fisher's Debt-Deflation Spiral: Why It Feeds on Itself

Economist Irving Fisher described this self-reinforcing mechanism in 1933, after living through the Great Depression, in what is now called the debt-deflation spiral. Chapter 1's Lesson 2 showed how rising collateral values create a self-reinforcing credit upswing. The debt-deflation spiral is the mirror image of that same mechanism running in reverse, and Chapter 4 covers the Great Depression itself as a full case study of it running unmanaged.

body.title: The Debt-Deflation Spiral, Step by Step

events.title: Distress Selling Begins
events.description: Borrowers who cannot refinance are forced to sell assets to raise cash and service debt.

events.title: Asset Prices Fall
events.description: That forced selling pushes down the price of the assets being sold, beyond what fundamentals alone would justify.

events.title: Collateral Values Shrink
events.description: Falling asset prices reduce the value of collateral backing other loans, triggering further margin calls and loan recalls elsewhere in the system.

events.title: Credit and Money Supply Contract
events.description: Lenders tighten further, loans get repaid faster than new ones are issued, and the total stock of credit and money in the system shrinks.

events.title: Prices Fall Across the Economy
events.description: Contracting money and credit reduce overall spending, pushing general price levels down: outright deflation.

events.title: The Real Debt Burden Rises
events.description: Because debts are fixed in nominal terms, falling prices increase the real burden of existing debt even though nothing about the debt contract has changed, worsening the very problem that started the spiral.

children.text: Why Cutting Rates to Zero Does Not Stop a Deflationary Spiral

markDefs.definition: The interest rate after adjusting for inflation, approximately equal to the nominal interest rate minus the inflation rate. It represents the true cost of borrowing, or the true return to a lender, in terms of actual purchasing power.

children.text: Step 6 in the spiral above explains something that otherwise looks paradoxical: a central bank can cut its nominal policy rate all the way to zero and still fail to relieve the pressure on borrowers. What actually matters to a borrower is the

, not the nominal one. Once deflation sets in, a 0% nominal rate combined with falling prices still produces a positive, and rising, real interest rate, which makes existing debt harder, not easier, to service in real terms. This is exactly why MP1 loses its power once a deflationary spiral is underway, and exactly why Chapter 2's MP2 and MP3 exist: they are attempts to fight deflation and restore real rates to a level that actually helps borrowers, once cutting the nominal rate alone has nothing left to give.

body.caption: Example: a 0% nominal policy rate combined with -5% inflation (deflation) produces a real rate of approximately +5%, even though the central bank has already cut as far as it conventionally can.

body.text: This is the specific trap a deflationary deleveraging sets: the tool that normally rescues an economy, cutting the nominal rate, becomes powerless exactly when it is needed most, because falling prices push the real rate up even as the nominal rate falls to zero. An unmanaged debt-deflation spiral does not correct itself through lower rates alone; it requires one or more of the four levers covered in the rest of this chapter.

children.text: Local Currency vs Foreign Currency Debt: Why the Difference Matters

One factor determines how much room a country has to manage its own deleveraging: whether its debt is denominated in its own currency or in a foreign one. A country that owes debt in its own currency has genuine, if imperfect, tools available: it can restructure that debt domestically, and its central bank can, in the most extreme cases, create the currency needed to help service it, at the cost of inflation. A country that owes debt in a foreign currency, US dollars being the most common example globally, cannot print dollars to solve a dollar-debt problem. That distinction is central to Chapter 4's case studies and explains why emerging-market debt crises have historically tended to be sharper and harder to manage than developed-market ones with debt denominated in their own currency.

body.title: What Sparks a Credit Event vs What Determines Whether It Spirals

columns.label: Common Onset Triggers
points: A large, visible, previously trusted borrower defaults
A sharper or faster rate hike than the market expected
A sudden currency depreciation for borrowers with foreign currency debt
A regulatory or accounting change that exposes previously hidden leverage

columns.label: What Determines Whether It Spirals
points: How much leverage had built up across the system before the trigger
How quickly authorities respond with one or more of the four levers
Whether the debt at risk is denominated in local or foreign currency
How interconnected the affected lenders and borrowers are with the rest of the financial system

body.title: Before You Move to the Four Levers
steps: Re-read the six-step debt-deflation spiral and identify which step India's 2018 IL&FS episode reached before policy intervention slowed it down

Check whether a debt situation you are analysing, personal, corporate, or sovereign, is denominated in local currency or foreign currency, since this changes what tools are actually available to manage it
Note the current inflation rate and current policy rate for an economy you follow, and calculate the approximate real interest rate using the formula in this lesson
Keep this real interest rate figure on hand; Chapter 3's next two lessons return to it directly when covering the four deleveraging levers

body.title: Spiral or Contained?
body.scenario: A mid-sized economy's largest private lender unexpectedly defaults on its bond obligations. In the following weeks, other lenders sharply cut back new lending to similar borrowers, several companies are forced to sell assets to raise cash, and asset prices in the affected sector fall 15%. The central bank responds within two weeks by cutting rates, providing emergency liquidity to solvent lenders, and publicly guaranteeing deposits at affected institutions.
body.prompt: Using the debt-deflation spiral and the two comparison columns in this lesson, assess how far this situation is likely to progress, and what about the central bank's response matters most.
body.modelAnswer: The situation has clearly reached Steps 1 through 3 of the debt-deflation spiral: distress selling, falling asset prices, and shrinking collateral values triggering tighter lending elsewhere. Whether it progresses to Steps 4 through 6, a genuine contraction in credit and money supply and outright deflation, depends heavily on the speed and credibility of the response. A two-week response time is fast by historical standards, and providing emergency liquidity to solvent lenders directly targets Step 4, preventing an otherwise-solvent institution from being forced into the same distress selling as the original defaulter simply because credit dried up. The deposit guarantee addresses confidence directly, which is what determines whether the spiral becomes self-reinforcing in the first place. The single most important detail is the speed of the liquidity response relative to how quickly confidence was breaking, since the entire spiral above is driven by a feedback loop that authorities can only interrupt while it is still gathering momentum, not after it has fully taken hold.

body.title: Check Your Understanding
body.question: An economy's nominal policy rate is at 0%, and inflation is running at -3% (outright deflation). What is the approximate real interest rate, and why does this matter for borrowers?
options: Approximately -3%, which makes debt easier to service
Approximately 0%, since the nominal rate is already at its floor
Approximately +3%, which makes debt harder to service even though the nominal rate cannot fall further
The real interest rate cannot be calculated when inflation is negative
body.explanation: Real interest rate approximately equals the nominal rate minus inflation, so 0% minus (-3%) equals approximately +3%. This is precisely why a central bank at the zero lower bound during deflation cannot rescue borrowers through rate cuts alone: the real burden of debt is rising even as the nominal rate sits at its floor, which is exactly the trap this lesson describes.

body.text: This lesson presents Irving Fisher's debt-deflation framework and Dalio's local versus foreign currency debt distinction for educational purposes and is not investment advice. The IL&FS example is a simplified summary of a well-documented 2018 event, presented for illustration; Chapter 5 covers it in more depth with sourced detail. Always verify specific dates, figures, and regulatory actions from RBI, SEBI, and NCLT public records before citing them professionally.

points: A deleveraging begins with a credit event: a trigger that breaks lenders' confidence and stops the refinancing that borrowers were relying on
India's 2018 IL&FS default is a real, compact example of a credit event triggering contagion across a connected sector, NBFCs and housing finance in that case

Fisher's debt-deflation spiral explains why an unmanaged deleveraging is self-reinforcing: distress selling lowers prices, which shrinks collateral, which contracts credit, which lowers prices further
A 0% nominal rate combined with deflation still produces a positive, rising real interest rate, which is why cutting rates to zero does not by itself stop a deflationary spiral
Whether debt is denominated in local or foreign currency determines how much room a country has to manage its own deleveraging, a distinction Chapter 4's case studies return to directly
Lessons 2 and 3 of this chapter cover the four levers, austerity, default and restructuring, wealth transfer, and money printing, used to interrupt this spiral once it starts
